packet_progression_note: One packet at a time. The next packet stays hidden until the current packet’s last required task has a passing deterministic check and Advance is unlocked. packet-diagram-algebraic also progressive-reveals inside the packet (diagram-ex960 before algebraic-ex960). packet-strategy is additional, not default: it stays hidden until Try another on sketch-try9120. packet-consolidation / fresh-hook-cts stays hidden until Consolidation.
chrome_note: Lean cycle chrome only: prediction commit, the active packet’s tool, Submit, hint, retry, and Advance when unlocked. Try another appears only on sketch-try9120 (unlocks strategy). No packet list, no sandbox explore-all, no Fresh-case on Action. Wonder-style advance chrome is an open call — this spec names advance_unlocks; it does not pick a Wonder control.

formative_handoff.note: Interaction-designer owns tools, representations, prompts, targets, and advance_unlocks. Formative-feedback-designer owns feedback_conditions, hint_sequence, message ids, FAME Mistakes (none in the approved bank — do not invent a signposted incorrect worked example here), and explanation-prompt message ids. Checking in this spec is deterministic-math handoff only: compare submitted evidence to the listed target; do not infer a brief misconception from a control value alone. Unrestricted predictions and interpretations are self-check or teacher-review — do not auto-grade free text. Packet Advance is unlocked only after the packet’s required task reports a pass; progression rules live here so feedback-spec can attach after_condition to the same task ids.

progression_rules.default: progressive-reveal one packet at a time after a passing check
progression_rules.within_packet_diagram_algebraic: diagram-ex960 pass unlocks algebraic-ex960; packet Advance unlocks only after algebraic-ex960 pass
progression_rules.strategy: not default; Try another on sketch-try9120 unlocks packet-strategy; default Advance from sketch-try9120 is packet-consolidation

student_action: Commit a prediction about the rewrite or the graph. Complete the square on the active packet’s tool (diagram, algebra, overlay, or sketch). Submit evidence. Read the check. Retry the same case or Advance to the next packet. The fountain photo is the hook figure only; it is not the graph tool.
changing_quantities: diagram side length and leftover constant
invariant: Completing the square rewrites f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c as f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k. The rewrite does not move the graph. Expanding and completing the square are inverse same-curve rewrites.
intended_observation: The completed-square writing makes the vertex (h, k), the axis x = h, and maximum versus minimum readable. A diagram shows the completed square and leftover before algebra. When a ≠ 1, factor a from the x^2 and x terms first. Simple rational b/a uses the same steps with fractions. Graphing technology shows one curve for both writings.
prediction_prompt: Before you move the board or write the next rewrite step, look at the standard-form equation in this packet. Will completing the square make a different curve, or the same one? What do you expect to be able to read once it is in vertex form?
interpretation_prompt: After you submitted, compare the two writings. What changed in the algebra? What stayed the same on the graph? How do you read the vertex from the completed-square writing?
fresh_case_prompt: Return to the fountain-arc situation with a new standard-form equation. Do not move the board yet. Complete the square, then name the vertex, the axis, and whether this is a maximum or a minimum. Set the graph to match that writing and submit. This case is Consolidation only.
sequence: Hook (Minds On figure only): fountain-arc photo. Need the high point; no vertex-form equation is given.

Packet sketch (A2.11 light): x^2 − 8x + 12 → (x − 4)^2 − 4; vertex (4, −4); axis x = 4; minimum (sketch-try9120). Try another unlocks strategy.

Consolidation only: fresh-hook-cts on y = −x^2 + 6x − 5 → −(x − 3)^2 + 4; vertex (3, 4); axis x = 3; maximum. No Fresh-case on Action.

packet_beat_map.beat: Shared-model L1 revisit: expand 3(x − 1)^2 + 4 to 3x^2 − 6x + 7, then complete the square back; both leave the graph unchanged (A2.7 REVIEW only).
Worked diagram then matching algebra on x^2 + 6x + 5. Progressive within packet: diagram side 3 leftover −4, then (x + 3)^2 − 4.
Factor a = −3 from the x terms first: −3x^2 − 6x − 1 → −3(x + 1)^2 + 2. Fracture forget-factor-a.
Complete the square for 2x^2 − 8x + 3 and confirm the overlay is the same graph as 2(x − 2)^2 − 5.
A2.11 light: CTS x^2 − 8x + 12 → (x − 4)^2 − 4; name vertex, axis, minimum; sketch those features only. Try another unlocks strategy.
Additional, not default. A: factor x^2 − 5x + 6. B: complete the square x^2 + 4x + 7. Criteria only; no formula.
Return to the fountain hook with y = −x^2 + 6x − 5 → −(x − 3)^2 + 4; vertex (3, 4); axis x = 3; maximum.

tasks.student_action: On the shared model, expand f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4 to standard form, then complete the square on that standard writing to recover vertex form. Submit both writings and confirm the overlay is one curve.
changing_quantities: standard b, c from the expand
tasks.invariant: 3(x − 1)^2 + 4 and 3x^2 − 6x + 7 are the same parabola. Completing the square undoes the expand; the graph does not move.
tasks.intended_observation: The Ministry A2.7 sample function can be written both ways. Completing the square is the inverse rewrite of Lesson 1’s expand, not a new curve. A2.7 is REVIEW only — do not new-teach expansion here.
tasks.prediction_prompt: The board can show f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4. If you expand it and then complete the square on the expanded writing, will you get a different parabola or the same one? Write that down before you change the board.
tasks.action_prompt: Expand f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4 into ax^2 + bx + c. Enter a, b, and c. Then start from that standard writing and complete the square. Enter a, h, and k. Submit both. Use the overlay to see whether the graphs coincide.
tasks.interpretation_prompt: Do the two writings sit on top of each other? If someone claimed completing the square moved the fountain-shaped curve, what on this board would you show them?

tasks.student_action: Use algebra tiles or an area diagram for f(x) = x^2 + 6x + 5. Split the six x-tiles so a square can be completed. Name the side length of that square and the leftover constant before writing vertex-form algebra.
tasks.invariant: The completed square uses half of the x-coefficient as its side. The leftover is the original constant minus that side squared. No vertex-form equation is required on this task.
tasks.intended_observation: Half of 6 is 3, so the square is 3 by 3. Leftover is 5 − 9 = −4. The picture is waiting for (x + 3)^2 − 4; that writing is the next task in this packet.
tasks.prediction_prompt: Look at x^2 + 6x + 5. Do not complete the square yet. How would you split the six x-tiles so you can make a square? What leftover do you expect once that square is filled?
tasks.action_prompt: On the diagram (or the static picture if the interactive is not built), complete the square for x^2 + 6x + 5. Enter the side length of the completed square and the leftover constant. Submit those two numbers before any vertex-form algebra.
tasks.interpretation_prompt: What in the picture is the 3? What is the −4? Why is the leftover not the original +5?

target.note: Half of 6 is 3; leftover 5 − 9 = −4. Bank mcf3m-m4-openstax-ia2e-ex960-diagram.

tasks.student_action: Rewrite f(x) = x^2 + 6x + 5 as (x − h)^2 + k by completing the square. Match each algebraic step to the completed-square picture from diagram-ex960.
tasks.invariant: a stays 1. Adding and subtracting 9 rewrites the same expression. The diagram side 3 is h with opposite sign in (x + 3); leftover −4 is k.
tasks.intended_observation: Half of 6 is 3; 3^2 = 9; add and subtract 9; f(x) = (x + 3)^2 − 4, so a = 1, h = −3, k = −4. Plus inside the brackets is not a vertex at positive x.
tasks.prediction_prompt: The diagram named side 3 and leftover −4. Before you write algebra, what vertex-form writing do you expect? Where will the vertex be?
tasks.action_prompt: Complete the square for f(x) = x^2 + 6x + 5. Enter a, h, and k so the live writing matches (x + 3)^2 − 4. Submit. Do not copy a live vertex line until after you have tried.
tasks.interpretation_prompt: How does (x + 3) match the side of the square? How does −4 match the leftover? If you plotted this writing on the original standard-form graph, would the curve move?

treat a Match click as a pass

tasks.student_action: Rewrite f(x) = x^2 + 2x − 3 as (x − h)^2 + k by completing the square. This is a you-do after the 9.60 worked pair; do not copy those numbers.
tasks.invariant: a stays 1. Half of 2 is 1, not 3. The leftover uses −3 minus 1^2.
tasks.intended_observation: Sign-of-b variation: half of 2 is 1; f(x) = (x + 1)^2 − 4, so a = 1, h = −1, k = −4. The 9.60 side 3 is not a template.
tasks.prediction_prompt: Look at f(x) = x^2 + 2x − 3. Do not write the square yet. What is half of 2? What leftover do you expect? Will the vertex have a positive or negative x-coordinate?

tasks.interpretation_prompt: How is this rewrite like x^2 + 6x + 5, and what changed because b is 2 instead of 6? How do you read h from (x + 1)?

tasks.student_action: Rewrite f(x) = −3x^2 − 6x − 1 as a(x − h)^2 + k. Factor −3 from the x^2 and x terms first. Keep the constant −1 outside that factor. Do not complete the square as if a were 1.
tasks.invariant: a = −3 stays in front of the completed square. The constant −1 is not factored. Balancing (b/2)^2 is multiplied by a when it is added outside.
tasks.intended_observation: Factor −3 from the x terms: −3(x^2 + 2x) − 1. Half of 2 is 1; the +1 inside is multiplied by −3 so add 3 outside; f(x) = −3(x + 1)^2 + 2. Forgetting to factor a breaks the inside of the square.
tasks.prediction_prompt: Look at f(x) = −3x^2 − 6x − 1. Do not complete the square yet. What must you factor out before you take half of anything? Will a stay −3?
tasks.action_prompt: Factor −3 from the x^2 and x terms, then complete the square. Enter a, h, and k. Submit when the writing is −3(x + 1)^2 + 2 or the matching parameters.
tasks.interpretation_prompt: If someone completed the square on −3x^2 − 6x as if a were 1, what inside the brackets would go wrong? Why is k = 2, not −1?

do_not: accept a = 1 or a = 3 as a match

factor −3 from the constant −1 as a required student step

tasks.student_action: Rewrite f(x) = x^2 + (1/2)x + 1 as (x − h)^2 + k by completing the square. Use the same steps as the integer-b cases; b/a is the simple rational 1/2. This is not Ministry wording.
tasks.invariant: Same CTS steps: half of b/a, square it, add and subtract. Fractions are not a different method.
tasks.prediction_prompt: Look at f(x) = x^2 + (1/2)x + 1. Do not invent an integer shortcut. What is half of 1/2? What will you add and subtract?
tasks.action_prompt: Complete the square. Enter a, h, and k. Fractions are expected (h = −1/4, k = 15/16). Submit.
tasks.interpretation_prompt: Which step was the same as x^2 + 2x − 3? Which numbers became fractions? If you expand (x + 1/4)^2 + 15/16, do you recover x^2 + (1/2)x + 1?

tasks.intended_observation: A) x^2 − 5x + 6 factors as (x − 2)(x − 3); intercepts 2 and 3 are friendly. B) x^2 + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)^2 + 3 does not factor over the reals; complete the square for the vertex (−2, 3). Discriminant talk is teacher-only, not a student lesson.

tasks.interpretation_prompt: What criterion did you use? When would you wait for a formula instead of forcing factoring or completing the square? (Waiting is allowed; teaching the formula is not.)

open_calls.title: Area-diagram implement versus static fallback
open_calls.decision_needed: Build jsxgraph-cts-area-diagram as an interactive tile/area board (split six x-tiles, complete the square, leftover visible) versus ship a static completed-square figure plus numeric inputs for side and leftover on diagram-ex960.
open_calls.constraint: Either path must run predict–submit–check with target {side: 3, leftover: -4}. Paper tiles remain the no-JS fallback. Do not block the packet on an unimplemented interactive.

fallback: Paper or static diagrams, no login and no remote tool. Shared model: expand 3(x − 1)^2 + 4 and complete the square back; check a few table points on one sketch. Diagram: for x^2 + 6x + 5, name side 3 and leftover −4, then write (x + 3)^2 − 4. You-do: x^2 + 2x − 3 → (x + 1)^2 − 4. Factor a: −3x^2 − 6x − 1 → −3(x + 1)^2 + 2. Rational: x^2 + (1/2)x + 1 → (x + 1/4)^2 + 15/16. Verify: 2x^2 − 8x + 3 and 2(x − 2)^2 − 5 share table points. Sketch: x^2 − 8x + 12 → vertex (4, −4), axis x = 4, minimum. Optional: A factor x^2 − 5x + 6; B complete the square x^2 + 4x + 7. Fresh case later: y = −x^2 + 6x − 5 — complete the square, name vertex (3, 4), axis x = 3, maximum, then sketch.
fallback_student: On paper, start with f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4. Expand it, then complete the square on the expanded writing. Check that a few table points still sit on the same sketch. For x^2 + 6x + 5, split the six x-tiles, name the side of the completed square and the leftover, then write vertex form. On your own, complete the square for x^2 + 2x − 3. Then factor −3 from the x terms of −3x^2 − 6x − 1 before you complete the square. Use the same steps for x^2 + (1/2)x + 1. For 2x^2 − 8x + 3, complete the square and check that both writings give the same outputs. For x^2 − 8x + 12, complete the square, name the vertex, the axis, and whether this is a maximum or a minimum, then sketch those features. If you try another: for x^2 − 5x + 6 and x^2 + 4x + 7, choose factoring or completing the square and say why. Later, a new equation: y = −x^2 + 6x − 5. Complete the square, name the high point, the axis, and whether this is a maximum or a minimum, then sketch.
